title: Dorothy Sayers: the Awake Mind as Author
author: Reynolds, John Mark
summary: Reynolds makes the case for including Dorothy Sayers in a 'great texts' curriculum despite conceding she never wrote a single work as towering as Hamlet or Pride and Prejudice. His argument is that some authors belong in a classical curriculum not because of one masterpiece but because the whole arc of a writing life — genius, quirks, failures, and even sins visible across it — models something worth studying, the way Shakespeare's uneven Henry VI still shows the Bard making his way. He recounts teaching Sayers's early detective novel Whose Body? to college seniors and finding it un-dated because Sayers relies on a stable moral framework and the still-legible conventions of the detective genre. He credits her nonfiction — Are Women Human? and The Lost Tools of Learning — with seeding both a conservative feminism and the contemporary classical-education revival. The piece closes by praising Sayers's range as evidence of 'a mind awake,' proposing her whole life, read as a term-long unit, as itself the pedagogical payoff.
points: Argues some writers deserve a place in a Great Books curriculum for the coherence of an entire life's output, not for any single masterpiece.
Credits Sayers's The Lost Tools of Learning specifically with inspiring 'the contemporary classical education program.'
Notes Sayers combined 'a deeply feminist traditionalism' with orthodox Christian belief, a model that doesn't sort neatly into modern ideological camps.
Uses Whose Body? (1923) as a test case for why some genre fiction ages better than serious fiction of the same era.
Frames a 'read nearly everything by one author in a term' seminar as pedagogically superior to sampling isolated famous essays.
quotes: Yet I would claim that Dorothy Sayers, like CS Lewis or Langston Hughes, can be read in a great texts program. The sum of the genius, the person behind the prose and poetry, is greater than any individual work.

This book is almost as close to Napoleon I as it is to us in time, but the novel does not feel dated to my college students. Sayers is both relying on Christian morality and on the creation of a genre, the detective novel, whose rules keep her prose (almost) timeless.
When she asks Are Women Human? or looks at the Lost Tools of Learning she also manages to stimulate a deeply conservative feminism and inspire the contemporary classical education program.
Sayers captures, however, a possibility that she lived: a deeply feminist traditionalism and a better vision for education than mere job training.

If Shakespeare had given us nothing greater than Henry VI (in all its uneven parts), then we might still read him to see the Bard of Avon who made a living, earned a title for his family, and yet also looked (fairly) deeply into the human condition. Dorothy Sayers is the equal of that Shakespeare.
